stem: A historian using Ferraro's self-description as evidence about the Democrats' 1984 campaign strategy should conclude that

options.text: It proves the Democratic Party had become the party of the working class in actual policy, not just in campaign rhetoric
options.misconception: A self-portrait in an acceptance speech shows how the campaign wanted to be seen, not what the party's actual policies became.

options.text: It was aimed mainly at winning Republican voters
options.misconception: An acceptance speech is delivered to the party's own convention — its first audience is fellow Democrats, not Republicans.

options.text: It is useless as evidence because candidates always exaggerate their backgrounds
options.misconception: A source being crafted for a purpose does not make it useless — sourcing analysis asks what a strategic source reveals.

options.text: It shows how the campaign wanted voters to see her — upward mobility embodied — rather than a neutral biography

rationales.A: Background: a self-portrait in an acceptance speech shows how the campaign wanted to be seen, not what the party's actual policies became.
rationales.B: Background: an acceptance speech is delivered to the party's own convention — its first audience is fellow Democrats, not Republicans.
rationales.C: Background: a source being crafted for a purpose does not make it useless — sourcing analysis asks what a strategic source reveals.
rationales.D: Background: Ferraro's biography — daughter of working Americans, child of an immigrant father — is the campaign's chosen frame: upward mobility embodied.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who wrote this portrait and why. An acceptance speech is a campaign document, not a diary.
2. Background: Ferraro's biography — daughter of working Americans, child of an immigrant father — is the frame the campaign chose.
3. Background: it tells a historian how the Democrats wanted voters to see her, not the neutral facts of her life.
4. A crafted source still counts as evidence — it just evidences the strategy, not the biography.
Remember: read a campaign speech for the frame, not the facts.

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Geraldine Ferraro, acceptance address, Democratic National Convention, July 19, 1984 (abridged). Post-1929 material is paraphrased, not quoted.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Geraldine Ferraro's vice-presidential nomination acceptance address, July 19, 1984: Ferraro described herself as the daughter of working Americans and of a mother whose highest hope was a future for her children. She told the Democratic convention that the future was within reach.
